title: Christian funerals (CCC 1680–1690)
hook: the Church accompanies the dead with hope and commends them to God

segments.voice: Yesterday, popular piety: processions, pilgrimages, rosaries, the faith of ordinary people. Your line was the people's faith. Today, the last day of How we celebrate. Day one thousand one hundred eleven.

The coffin comes in at the back of the church, and the priest meets it at the door. He sprinkles it with water, the way water was poured on this person at baptism, long ago, maybe in this same building. A white cloth is spread over the wood. Nobody can tell from the outside whether the person in the box was rich or poor. The family walks behind, eyes down. A candle burns by the altar, the one that was lit at Easter. Every gesture is saying something. Today we listen to what a Catholic funeral says, from the door to the last goodbye.
screen: `MET AT THE DOOR.` → `WATER, AS AT BAPTISM.` → `A WHITE CLOTH, A CANDLE.`

segments.voice: The Catechism begins with hope. For a Christian, it says, death is seen in the light of Christ's death and resurrection. Jesus says to Martha, in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in me, although he be dead, shall live." That's the key the whole funeral is played in. The Catechism says the funeral doesn't give the dead person a sacrament. It expresses the Church's communion with them, gathers the living, and proclaims eternal life. Then it walks through the rite, and the shape is worth knowing. First, the greeting. In the rite, the community welcomes the person one last time, at the door, as it once welcomed them at baptism. Words of comfort and hope are spoken to the family. Second, the liturgy of the word. Scripture is read, even in grief, because the Church holds that God's word speaks into death too. Wisdom, in the Douay-Rheims, says: "the souls of the just are in the hand of God." Third, the Eucharist. The Church offers the Mass for the one who has died, and Catholics believe this prayer helps them, and that the bond between the living and the dead isn't broken. Fourth, the farewell. At the end, the Church commends the person to God. The Catechism calls it the last farewell, the community's final goodbye to one of its members before the body goes to the grave. A commendation is a handing over: here is someone we loved; we place them in your hands. Today also closes Part Two, How we celebrate. The liturgy, signs and songs and sacred time, the church building, the sacraments from baptism to the Eucharist, penance, anointing, Holy Orders and marriage, sacramentals and the people's devotions, and now the farewell. The Church's celebrating runs from the font to the grave.
screen: `DEATH IN THE LIGHT OF THE RESURRECTION.` · `THE GREETING AT THE DOOR.` · `THE WORD AND THE EUCHARIST.` · `THE FAREWELL: COMMENDED TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: attend or remember a funeral. If there's a funeral you can go to soon, consider going, even if you knew the family more than the one who died. If not, remember one you've been to. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the room: the music, the faces, the moment the coffin left. Bring back the person. Say their name quietly. If you pray, you can commend them to God, in your own silence or with words of the Church you already know. If you don't, simply remember them with gratitude until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Christian funerals. The Church meets the dead at the door, reads the word, offers the Eucharist, and, at the farewell, commends them to God, in the hope of the resurrection. Today's word.
Your line: commended to God. Today, say the name of someone you've lost, aloud or in your head, and hand them over, once more. Day one thousand one hundred eleven.

howItsDone: A Catholic funeral usually includes a vigil or wake, a funeral Mass with the coffin received at the church door and covered with a white pall, and a final commendation before burial, with prayers at the graveside.
